concepts.name: Pydantic AI: typed output and generic agents
Pydantic AI: dependencies, `RunContext` and tool schemas
When you would pick each framework

questions.prompt: `agent = Agent("openai:gpt-5.2", output_type=CityInfo)`, then `result = agent.run_sync("Tell me about Paris")`. How do you get the validated `CityInfo`?

choices.text: `CityInfo.model_validate_json(result.text)`
`result.messages[-1]`
`result.output`
`CityInfo(**result)`

questions.explanation: `output_type` is the structured type the model must return at the end of a run, and Pydantic AI validates it for you. The validated object is on `result.output`. Parsing text yourself would throw away the validation and retry behaviour the framework gives you.

questions.prompt: An agent needs dependencies of type `Foobar` and produces `list[str]`. What is its type, as a type checker sees it?

choices.text: `Agent[Foobar, list[str]]`
`Agent[list[str], Foobar]`
`Agent[RunContext[Foobar], list[str]]`
`Agent[Foobar]`, since output types aren't tracked

questions.explanation: The docs say agents are generic in their dependency and output types, in that order, and give this exact example: `Agent[Foobar, list[str]]`. That is what lets a type checker catch a tool that expects the wrong deps or code that misuses the output.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `@agent.tool` and `@agent.tool_plain`?

choices.text: `@agent.tool_plain` tools are hidden from the model and only callable from your own code
`@agent.tool` functions must be async, while `@agent.tool_plain` functions must be sync
`@agent.tool_plain` skips Pydantic argument validation, so its tools run with lower per-call overhead
`@agent.tool` functions take `RunContext` first, for deps; `@agent.tool_plain` functions don't

questions.explanation: Both register tools the model can call, with validated arguments. `@agent.tool` is the default because most tools need the agent context: they receive `RunContext`, and `ctx.deps` carries your dependencies. `@agent.tool_plain` is for tools that need no context.

questions.prompt: Given `@agent.tool async def get_balance(ctx: RunContext[Deps], account_id: int) -> float` with a Google-style docstring describing `account_id`, what goes into the tool schema the model sees?

choices.text: Both `ctx` and `account_id`, since every function parameter becomes a field
`account_id` as an integer, described from the docstring; `ctx` is left out
Only the function name and docstring; the model infers the parameters
`account_id` as a string, since JSON Schema has no integer type

questions.explanation: Pydantic AI builds the schema from the function signature using every parameter except `RunContext`, and uses griffe to pull parameter descriptions from the docstring (Google, NumPy or Sphinx style). JSON Schema has an `integer` type, so the annotation `int` is kept.

questions.prompt: Inside a tool, you `raise ModelRetry("Unknown account id; call list_accounts first")`. What does Pydantic AI do?

choices.text: It returns the message to the model to retry; past the limit it raises `UnexpectedModelBehavior`
It ends the run immediately and re-raises `ModelRetry` to your code for you to handle
It retries the same tool call with the same arguments until it succeeds or times out
It logs the message as a warning and returns `None` to the model as the tool's result

questions.explanation: A tool retry is a message to the model saying the call didn't work and why, so it can correct itself. `ModelRetry`, invalid tool arguments, a tool timeout and calling a tool that doesn't exist all trigger one. The default budget is 1 retry; when it is used up the run raises `UnexpectedModelBehavior`.

questions.prompt: The model's final answer fails validation against your `output_type`. Explain what Pydantic AI does, how you control it, and how you would add a check that the schema alone can't express.

model_answer.summary: A validation failure triggers an output retry: the error goes back to the model so it can fix its answer. The retry budget defaults to 1 and is configurable; when it runs out the run raises `UnexpectedModelBehavior`. For custom checks, an output validator can raise `ModelRetry`.
key_points: A failed validation of the output triggers an output retry, sending the error back to the model
The default retry budget is 1; the agent's `retries` setting changes it (a plain int sets both tool and output budgets)
When the budget is exhausted the run raises `UnexpectedModelBehavior`
An output validator (or output function) can raise `ModelRetry` to ask for a corrected answer on business rules

questions.explanation: The retries page lists what triggers each kind of retry and says a bare int sets both budgets. Retries cost extra model calls, so a higher budget trades cost for reliability. Handle `UnexpectedModelBehavior` in your code so a stubborn failure doesn't crash the request.

questions.prompt: Which three attributes must every CrewAI agent have?

choices.text: `name`, `instructions` and `tools`
`role`, `task` and `model`
`role`, `goal` and `backstory`
`goal`, `expected_output` and `agent`

questions.explanation: CrewAI agents are role-based: `role` defines the agent's function, `goal` its objective, and `backstory` gives context and personality. `description` and `expected_output` belong to tasks, not agents. `allow_delegation` is optional and defaults to `False`.

questions.prompt: In a sequential crew, a `research` task runs before a `write` task. How does the writer get the research?

choices.text: You pass it yourself: read the research output and feed it into the `inputs` dict of `kickoff()`
Each task's output becomes context for the next; a task's `context` list picks specific tasks
Only if every agent sets `allow_delegation=True`, so the writer can ask the researcher
It can't: tasks in a crew are independent, so the writer must redo the research

questions.explanation: In the sequential process the output of one task serves as context for the next. A task's `context=[...]` attribute names which earlier task outputs it should receive, which also allows non-adjacent dependencies. Each task needs a `description` and an `expected_output`.

questions.prompt: What does a crew with `process=Process.hierarchical` require?

choices.text: A `manager_llm` or `manager_agent` that assigns tasks and reviews outputs
An agent assigned to every task in advance, as in the sequential process
A Flow with a `@router()` method that picks which agent runs next
`allow_delegation=True` on every agent so they can hand work to each other

questions.explanation: The hierarchical process needs a manager, given as `manager_llm` or `manager_agent`. The manager allocates tasks to agents based on their capabilities, reviews outputs and judges completion, so tasks don't need an agent assigned up front. That is the main difference from the sequential process.

questions.prompt: Compare CrewAI Crews and Flows. When would you wrap a crew inside a Flow?

model_answer.summary: A Crew is a team of role-based agents working through tasks under a process. A Flow is event-driven orchestration, with `@start`, `@listen` and `@router` methods and managed state, that can call crews and plain code. Use a Flow when you need explicit branching, state across steps, or several crews in one pipeline.
key_points: A Crew groups agents and tasks and runs them with a sequential or hierarchical process
A Flow wires methods together with `@start()` entry points and `@listen()` methods that run when another method finishes
`@router()` gives conditional branching based on a method's output
Flow state can be structured (a Pydantic model) or unstructured
Wrap crews in a Flow when control flow and state must be explicit rather than left to the agents

questions.explanation: The Flows docs present crews as focused units of work and Flows as the layer that connects tasks, manages state and controls execution. This split is useful in a comparison table: CrewAI alone covers both agent-led teamwork and code-led orchestration.

questions.prompt: Fill in one row of your comparison table for each framework: Pydantic AI, CrewAI and LangGraph. For each, say what it is best at and one situation where you would pick it.

model_answer.summary: Pydantic AI suits type-safe agents with validated, structured output in ordinary Python. CrewAI suits role-based teams of agents working through tasks. LangGraph suits explicit, stateful graphs that must persist and resume.
key_points: Pydantic AI: agents are generic in deps and output type, and output is validated with retries
Pick Pydantic AI for a single agent or service whose structured result code depends on
CrewAI: agents defined by role, goal and backstory, running tasks in a sequential or hierarchical process (Flows for explicit control)
LangGraph: a low-level `StateGraph` of nodes and edges, with persistence for long-running, resumable, human-in-the-loop work
The choice follows the requirement: typed output, role-based collaboration, or explicit durable control flow

questions.explanation: Each framework's docs lead with a different core idea: typing for Pydantic AI, roles for CrewAI, graphs and persistence for LangGraph. A strong row names the feature and a concrete case. Answers that only say one is "simpler" or "more powerful" can't be checked.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of framework and feature matches that framework's own docs?

choices.text: Pydantic AI: a hierarchical process with a manager agent
LangGraph: agents generic in their dependency and output types
CrewAI: a `StateGraph` of nodes and edges compiled before running
CrewAI: agents defined by `role`, `goal` and `backstory`

questions.explanation: Role, goal and backstory are CrewAI's required agent attributes. The hierarchical process with a manager is also CrewAI. Generic `Agent[Deps, Output]` typing is Pydantic AI. `StateGraph` with nodes and edges is LangGraph. Mixing these up is easy after reading three sets of docs, which is why the comparison table helps.
